title: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible orderings (permutations) using backtracking.
shortTitle: Permutations: backtracking with a used[] array
keyPoints: Fill positions one by one with unused elements; when the path reaches length n, record it as a complete permutation.
A boolean used[] array marks elements already placed in the current path.
Unlike subsets, there is no start index because every position draws from any unused element.
Time is O(n * n!) because there are n! permutations, each of length n to copy.
The swap-based variant avoids the used[] array by swapping elements into position.
This pattern appears in scheduling problems where every ordering must be evaluated.

s1_definition.oneliner: Fill positions one by one with unused elements; when full, record the ordering and backtrack: n! results.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Depth-first backtracking** – at each position, choose an element not yet used in the current path.
- **used[] array** – a boolean array tracking which elements are currently placed.
- **Record at full length** – when the path size equals n, snapshot it as a complete permutation.
- **Undo on backtrack** – remove the element and unmark used[] before trying the next candidate.
- **O(n * n!)** – n! permutations, each requiring O(n) to copy.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must try every order in which n settlement batches could run when order affects the outcome. At each slot Pankaj picks a batch not yet used, fills all slots, records that ordering, then unpicks to try a different arrangement.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Backtracking tree for [Interest, Fees, Notify]:

  []
  ├── [Interest]
  │   ├── [Interest, Fees]
  │   │   └── [Interest, Fees, Notify] ← record
  │   └── [Interest, Notify]
  │       └── [Interest, Notify, Fees] ← record
  ├── [Fees]
  │   ├── [Fees, Interest]
  │   │   └── [Fees, Interest, Notify] ← record
  │   └── [Fees, Notify]
  │       └── [Fees, Notify, Interest] ← record
  └── [Notify]
      ├── [Notify, Interest]
      │   └── [Notify, Interest, Fees] ← record
      └── [Notify, Fees]
          └── [Notify, Fees, Interest] ← record

  Total: 3! = 6 permutations
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations is the backtracking problem for generating every ordering of distinct elements. I carry the current partial ordering plus a boolean used array, and whenever the path reaches length n I record it. Otherwise I loop over every index, skip used ones, choose the element, recurse, and undo both actions.

The key structural difference from subsets is that there is no start index: every position draws from any unused element, which produces orderings rather than combinations.

In my project at National Bank of India, a simulation had to evaluate every possible run order of a small set of end-of-day settlement batches to assess order-dependent risk. This backtracking enumerated them cleanly.

The swap-based variant drops the used[] array by swapping elements into position, saving space but sacrificing clarity. Both produce the same n! results.

Remember one sentence: at each position pick any unused element, recurse, undo, and record only when the path is full.
